title: Is tone deafness hereditary?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss tone deafness (amusia), opening with a tangent about "My Way killings" in the Philippines and other karaoke-related violence. They explain pitch as frequency, the difference between tone deafness and perfect (absolute) pitch versus relative pitch, and note that tone deaf people reproduce what they hear faithfully. They describe an online tone deafness test they took and their scores, and discuss how altitude affects pitch. They cover the genetic basis (identical twins scoring similarly), the arcuate fasciculus study, a 2007 Harvard Health Letter item on white matter connecting the frontal and temporal lobes, a UCSF genetic study, and other reasons someone may sing poorly (vocal control, imitation, memory). The episode ends with housekeeping: Facebook likes, October Atlanta events including a trivia night, and a call for karaoke stories.

entities.name: University of New York at Buffalo

segments.title: Opening banter and My Way killings
segments.summary: The hosts open with light banter, then Josh introduces the 'My Way killings' in the Philippines, where violence has been linked to people singing or being jeered for singing the Sinatra song, and notes a Thai case involving John Denver's Country Roads.

segments.title: What tone deafness is: pitch, perfect pitch and relative pitch
segments.summary: Chuck explains that tone deafness (amusia) is not about hearing loss, that tone deaf people reproduce what they hear faithfully, and that about one in twenty can't carry a tune. They explain pitch as frequency and distinguish perfect (absolute) pitch, which is rare, from relative pitch, which is common. Famous musicians with perfect pitch are named.

segments.title: Online tone deafness test
segments.summary: The hosts describe an online tone deafness test with same-or-different listening items. Josh scored 27 of 30 on both parts, about 78 percent, and Chuck rated himself average as a singer.

segments.title: Pitch and altitude
segments.summary: Chuck notes that pitch is not constant: a piano string's vibration differs at higher altitude because of air pressure. They discuss how people who are tone deaf fail to hear small pitch differences, comparing it to color blindness, which exists in degrees.

segments.title: Causes: heredity, brain structure and other reasons for poor singing
segments.summary: Chuck says tone deafness appears hereditary, with identical twins scoring similarly. The arcuate fasciculus is described as a possible factor, with smaller fibers in tone deaf people. A 2007 Harvard Health Letter item on less white matter between the frontal and temporal lobes is covered. A UCSF genetic study is mentioned. Training is said not to help. A University of New York at Buffalo and Simon Fraser University study proposes other reasons for poor singing: vocal control, imitation, and memory.

segments.title: Digression on Frank Black and Paul Data
segments.summary: The hosts talk about seeing Frank Black live, with the Doolittle set, and then describe a young violinist named Paul Data who plays along with a DJ cousin to tribe Called Quest and Fat Boys-style tracks.

segments.title: Facebook and event announcements
segments.summary: The hosts ask listeners to like the Facebook page and announce an October Atlanta Henry Clay show and a celebrity trivia night, and skip listener mail this week.

segments.title: Sign-off and karaoke story request
segments.summary: The hosts ask listeners to email karaoke stories and close the episode with the standard sign-off.
